items.prompt: Which schedule is an example of spaced practice?
choices: One six-hour session on the night before the test
Reading one page six times in a single hour
Studying only on the last day in short bursts
Six 30-minute sessions spread across four weeks
items.explanation: Spaced practice spreads reviews over time instead of packing them into one block.

items.prompt: What is massed practice usually called in everyday language?
choices: Chunking
Pacing
Cramming
Skimming
items.explanation: Packing most of the study into one block is cramming.

items.prompt: Maya and Diego both study 3 hours in total. What differs?
choices: How many words they study
How long the test lasts
When the hours happen
Which words are on the test
items.explanation: Words, total hours and test day are the same. Only the schedule differs.

items.prompt: What does spaced repetition mean?
choices: Repeating one fact aloud many times in a row
Studying the same amount at the same hour daily
Reviewing once right after learning and then stopping
Reviewing at growing intervals instead of all at once
items.explanation: Spacing stretches the intervals between reviews over time.

items.prompt: A gardener waters heavily once, then leaves for a month. What does this resemble?
choices: Spaced practice
Cramming
Active recall
Retrieval practice
items.explanation: One large dose followed by nothing is the massed pattern, like one long study block.

items.prompt: After a single long session, what happens to the memory as days pass?
choices: It strengthens by itself over time
It stays exactly as strong
It fades by itself
It fades only if you sleep poorly
items.explanation: Without review, memory fades. Reviews are what interrupt that fading.

items.prompt: Which statement about total study time is correct?
choices: Only the number of hours matters
Timing matters as much as hours
Timing matters for easy items only
Timing never matters at all
items.explanation: Equal hours can give very different results depending on how they are spread out.

items.prompt: How does cramming usually feel while you do it?
choices: Hard, as every fact is fading
Confusing, as nothing is familiar
Painful, as each review is too frequent
Smooth, as everything is still fresh
items.explanation: Cramming feels smooth, which is part of why it is tempting and why it protects so little later.

items.prompt: Learner A studies 4 hours in one night. Learner B studies 4 hours as eight 30-minute sessions over three weeks. Both are tested three weeks later. What is the best prediction?
choices: B, because each review reset the fading
A retains more, because the single block was longer
They tie, because total study time was identical
A retains more, because the material stayed fresh
items.explanation: Equal total time does not give equal retention. B's reviews each lifted the memory and slowed the next fade, while A's memory faded undisturbed for three weeks.
items.reference:
Same 3 hours, two schedules
🌙 Massed: one 3-hour block, 10% on test day
📅 Spaced: six 30-minute sessions, 90% on test day (teaching numbers)
Why: Total hours were equal, so the difference came from when the hours happened.
items.learnMore:
When you study matters as much as how long

Cramming leaves nothing to interrupt the fading after the session ends. Spaced reviews each lift the memory back up and slow the next fade.

Common mistake

Assuming that more total hours always means better retention.
items.reflection: Think of something you once crammed and lost within weeks. What would a spread-out version of that effort have looked like?

items.prompt: Both learners are tested the morning after studying, not weeks later. Why might cramming look fine in that case?
choices: Cramming builds stronger long-term memory than spacing
Spacing only works when the test is far away
Fading is slower in the first hour than later
Little time has passed for the memory to fade
items.explanation: Retention right after study is high for both methods. The gap shows up weeks later, after undisturbed fading has had time to act.

Only the timing differs, so timing explains the gap

items.prompt: What is retrieval practice?
choices: Looking at the material again and again
Copying notes onto paper
Trying to recall the answer yourself
Listening to the material while walking
items.explanation: Retrieval means producing the answer from memory, not just seeing it again.

items.prompt: What is active recall in a flashcard setting?
choices: Reading both sides of the card together
Answering before you flip the card
Sorting cards by color
Flipping the card then reading it twice
items.explanation: Hide the answer, try first, then check.

items.prompt: Which review is rereading?
choices: Covering the answer and writing it from memory
Explaining the idea aloud with no notes
Answering a practice question before looking
Reading question and answer together
items.explanation: Seeing the answer first turns the review into recognition.

items.prompt: Why can rereading feel like it is working?
choices: Familiarity on the page feels like knowing
The words get shorter each time you read
Your memory is strengthened most by reading
Rereading forces you to guess each answer
items.explanation: Familiarity is easy to mistake for being able to recall without the page.

items.prompt: Which is the better first step when reviewing a card?
choices: Try to recall the answer
Read the answer slowly
Skim the whole deck
Count how many cards remain
items.explanation: The attempt to recall is what strengthens memory, so it should come before checking.

items.prompt: Retrieval practice is best described as a...
choices: A single product you must buy
A schedule that sets the review dates
A broad principle
A type of note-taking layout on paper
items.explanation: It is the principle. Active recall is a common way to carry it out.

items.prompt: Which feels harder in the moment but works better?
choices: Reading your notes from top to bottom
Highlighting the key lines in yellow
Trying to answer before checking
Copying the answer once you see it
items.explanation: The effort of pulling the answer up is the useful part.

items.prompt: What is the key difference between recall and rereading?
choices: How many minutes the review takes
Whether you try before seeing the answer
How many pages the material covers in all
Whether you review in the morning or at night
items.explanation: Both involve the same material. Only the order of seeing and trying differs.

items.prompt: Two students review the same cards on the same days for the same time. One tries each answer first. The other reads both sides together. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The first, because retrieval does the work
The second retains more, because they saw more answers
They retain the same, because timing was identical
The first retains more, because they studied longer
items.explanation: Timing and total time were held equal. What differs is the type of review, and the attempt to recall is what does most of the strengthening.
items.reference:
Two reviews, one order flipped
🧠 Active recall: question, try from memory, then check
📄 Rereading: see question and answer together, nod
Why: Trying to pull the answer from memory is the work that strengthens it, so order matters.
items.learnMore:
Pulling beats looking

Retrieval practice makes memory reconstruct the answer. Rereading shows the answer first, so the review becomes recognition, which feels fluent but builds much less.

Common mistake

Treating a page that looks familiar as proof that you could produce the answer yourself.
items.reflection: Pick something you recently reread. How would you quiz yourself on it tomorrow without opening it first?

items.prompt: A learner reviews notes on a perfect schedule but only rereads them. What is the most likely result?
choices: No benefit at all compared to cramming
The same benefit as full active recall
Worse than cramming, since rereading harms memory
Better than cramming, less than active recall
items.explanation: Good timing still helps, but passive rereading adds less to each review than a genuine attempt to recall.

Feeling sure is a reliable sign of knowing

Yes, you should skip checking and move on
No, the attempt still strengthens how the answer is stored
No, but only if you guess correctly within a minute
items.explanation: The effort of trying to recall, even when it fails, makes the following check more effective. Checking afterward closes the gap.

items.prompt: What is the forgetting curve?
choices: The speed at which you read new material
How memory fades when nothing is reviewed
The number of cards in one study deck
The order in which facts are first learned
items.explanation: It describes fading with no review.

items.prompt: When does forgetting happen fastest?
choices: After about a month
Only when you sleep
Right after learning
Evenly through the whole period
items.explanation: The curve is steep at first and slower later.

items.prompt: What does a successful review do to retention?
choices: Lowers it a little
Leaves it unchanged
Locks it at zero
Lifts it back up
items.explanation: A successful review resets retention and makes the next fade gentler.

items.prompt: After several successful reviews, the next fade is...
choices: Faster than before
Slower than before
Exactly the same
Impossible to predict
items.explanation: Each review flattens the curve that follows.

items.prompt: In the unit's teaching numbers, retention one day after learning with no review is about...
items.explanation: The teaching curve goes 100, 55, 42, 30 and so on. It is not a measurement.

items.prompt: Why do review intervals stretch out over time?
choices: Learners get bored of short gaps
Longer gaps are always the best choice
Short gaps are not allowed by the model
A sturdier memory needs fewer reminders
items.explanation: As each fade slows, the next review can wait longer.

items.prompt: Which word describes a review lifting retention back up?
choices: Decay
Flatten
Reset
Drift
items.explanation: Reset means retention is lifted again. Decay is the fading itself.

items.prompt: With no review, the unit's teaching curve falls to about what by day 28?
items.explanation: It matches Maya's result of about 10% in the simplified model.

items.prompt: Retention drops from 100% to 55% on day 1, then from 55% to 42% on day 2. What does this show about the curve?
choices: It falls fastest at first, then slows
The drop is identical in size each day
The drop grows larger as the days go on
The drop ends entirely right after day 2
items.explanation: The first day loses 45 points and the second only 13, so the loss per day shrinks. That is a curve, not a straight line.
items.reference:
The shape of fading
📉 Steep right after learning, then a long slow slope
🔁 Each successful review resets it and flattens the next fall
Why: Memory does not fade at a constant rate, so the first stretch after learning matters most.
items.learnMore:
Why review intervals stretch

Each success makes the memory sturdier, so the next fade is slower. That is why a first review comes soon and later reviews can wait longer.

Common mistake

Picturing forgetting as a straight line, which hides that the early drop is the steepest.
items.reflection: Think of a fact you learned long ago and still know. What reviews, formal or not, probably flattened its curve?

Less is left to lose, not less reason to review

Impossible without rereading

items.explanation: Recall that takes a little work shows the memory is fading but still reachable.

choices: The review is probably too late
The review is probably too soon
The review is perfectly timed
The memory has failed entirely
items.explanation: Instant recall means little has faded, so the review adds little.

items.prompt: You cannot start without rereading. What does this suggest?
choices: The review is probably too soon
The review is perfectly timed
The material was never in the deck
The review is probably too late
items.explanation: If nothing can be recalled, you are relearning rather than reinforcing.

items.prompt: You remember the first half but need a hint. What is the best move?

Try first, then check the missing piece
Reread the whole card twice
Reread the entire card three times in a row
items.explanation: A partial recall is still useful. Try first and then fill in the gap.

Painful, because reviews are too frequent
Smooth, because everything is still fresh
Random, because order keeps changing
items.explanation: The smoothness is the reason it feels productive and why it protects little later.

items.prompt: Which term means reviewing before the memory has faded much?
choices: Well timed
Too late
Too soon
Overdue
items.explanation: A review while recall is still effortless adds little.

items.prompt: Do you need an exact timer to time reviews?
choices: Yes, you need a stopwatch for every card
No, effort is a useful signal
Yes, reviews must happen on exact hours
No, because timing never matters at all
items.explanation: Rough spacing plus the feel of the effort is enough to start.

items.prompt: Is extra mental effort during review a downside?
choices: Yes, it means you should stop at once
Yes, it shows the cards are useless
No, it is how reviews strengthen memory
No, but only when the effort lasts an hour
items.explanation: The effort of pulling up a fading memory is the mechanism.

items.prompt: You review a card and the answer comes after a three-second pause. How should you read that?
choices: A good sign: memory faded but is reachable
A bad sign: the review should have been earlier
A neutral sign that tells you nothing
A bad sign: you should restart the whole deck
items.explanation: A pause before a correct answer shows effortful recall, which is the signature of a well-timed review.
items.reference:
Reading the effort signal
⚡ Instant, no effort: probably too soon
⏳ Answer after a pause: well timed
🧱 Cannot start without rereading: probably too late
Why: Recall that takes a little work shows the memory is fading but still reachable.
items.learnMore:
Effort is a signal, not a failure

A review is well placed when the answer is still there but needs effort to reach. Too early adds little, and too late turns into relearning.

Common mistake

Treating the extra effort of a well-timed review as a sign that the schedule is wrong.
items.reflection: Think of the last time you recalled something with effort and succeeded. Was that the moment a review would have helped most?

items.explanation: Spacing still helps, so he beats zero reviews. Without the attempt to recall, each session reinforces less than in the original schedule.
items.reference:
Diego's reviews, teaching numbers
📅 Days 2, 4, 8, 16, 24, then test on day 28
📈 Just before each review: 55, 65, 72, 78, 85, then 90 at the test
🧮 Demo: 10 + 5 x 16 = 90% with 5 reviews, 10% with none
Why: Each review lifts memory and flattens the next fall, so the dip before the next review gets shallower.
items.learnMore:
Reading a spaced schedule

Look at the retention just before each review. If that number climbs, the memory is becoming sturdier. The gap alone is only half the story.

Common mistake

Comparing only days since last review and ignoring how sturdy the memory already was.
items.reflection: If you built a review schedule for something you need to keep for a year, where would your first three reviews go and why?
